U.S. Supreme Court

Advocacy groups file amicus brief in third country deportation case

U.S. Supreme Court to hear oral arguments on Dec. 9

Published

24 hours ago

on

November 23, 2026

By

Michael K. Lavers
U.S. Supreme Court (Washington Blade photo by Michael Key)
  • Share
  • Tweet
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 33:15
Instaread

Seven LGBTQ advocacy groups on Monday filed an amicus brief in a case that challenges the Trump-Vance administration’s policy of deporting people to countries to which they have no ties.

The U.S. Supreme Court in September in a 6-3 ruling said the White House can continue the third country deportation policy.

The National Immigration Litigation Alliance, along with Human Rights First and the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project, filed a class action lawsuit against the policy in 2025. The U.S. Supreme Court is scheduled to hear oral arguments in the case, Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., on Dec. 9.

Lambda Legal, Immigration Equality, Oasis Legal Services, the Council for Global Equality, Outright International, Rainbow Railroad, and ORAM (Organization for Refuge, Asylum and Migration) are the groups that filed the amicus brief. They argue the deportation of LGBTQ migrants to a third country — especially those that criminalize consensual same-sex sexual relations — places them at increased risk.

“A U.S. judge found that these refugees would likely be persecuted or tortured if sent home, and the administration responded by sending many of them somewhere else equally dangerous, without a warning and without a hearing,” said Immigration Equality Law and Policy Director Bridget Crawford, who co-wrote the brief, in a statement the Washington Blade received on Monday.

“The law is clear that the government may not deport people to countries where they face persecution or torture, and it must give them a fair opportunity to raise that fear first,” added Crawford. “These safeguards are being ignored. Notice and a meaningful chance to object are required by federal law, by our treaty obligations, and by the Constitution, and for LGBTQ refugees, they are the difference between safety and the threat of imprisonment, violence, or death.”

Oasis Legal Services Staff Attorney celia meredith said “third-country deportations place LGBTQ+ migrants in grave danger.” meredith, who does not capitalize their name, further notes their organization “has worked with many LGBTQ+ migrants who fled harm in their home countries and tried to find safety in a third country like Mexico, only to suffer brutal persecution.”

“Without a correct outcome in this case, LGBTQ+ immigrants will be sent to third countries where being LGBTQ+ is illegal or where their identities place a target on their backs,” said meredith. “They will be sent without community support, without government protection, and at very high risk of being harmed.”

Council for Global Equality Managing Director Keifer Buckingham noted the case of a gay Ghanaian asylum seeker from Ghana who the Trump-Vance administration flew to Equatorial Guinea — “a country where LGBTQI+ people face high levels of violence and torture” — before he was “forcibly deported back to Ghana.”

Ghana is among the countries in which consensual same-sex sexual relations remain criminalized.

Lawmakers in the African country earlier this year approved a bill that would, among other things, criminalize LGBTQ allyship. Ghanaian media reports indicate MPs this month rescinded its passage in order to address “inconsistencies” in it.

“The Trump administration’s practice of third country removals — including the usage of opaque bilateral agreements with countries that routinely abuse human rights — is the very embodiment of what has been a hateful and inhumane immigration policy over the last two years,” said Buckingham. “We hope the Supreme Court will see this policy for what it is: not only cruel, but illegal.”

Oliver Williams, the U.S. policy and advocacy officer for Rainbow Railroad, said the U.S. “has a legal and moral duty not to send people to countries where they will face imminent danger.” ORAM Executive Director Steve Roth made a similar argument.

“LGBTQ+ people who seek protection in the United States place enormous trust in its laws and institutions,” he said.

“For those who have already been granted protection by an immigration judge, being sent to another potentially dangerous country without a meaningful opportunity to be heard is a profound betrayal of that trust,” added Roth. “It also undermines the credibility of the United States and its commitment to protecting people fleeing persecution.”

U.S. Supreme Court

Supreme Court faces new questions over trans rights and equal protection

One case sent back to lower court as SCOTUS considers taking up another

Published

6 days ago

on

November 18, 2026

By

Joe Reberkenny
Pride and American Flags flying in front of the Supreme Court before the United States v. Skrmetti decision. (Washington Blade photo by Michael Key)

The U.S. Supreme Court has taken action in one case and is being asked to review another, two legal challenges that could have significant implications for transgender people in the United States, including those incarcerated in state prisons and serving in the U.S. military.

The cases, Roybal v. Griffith and Talbott v. USA, involve separate challenges to policies affecting trans people. Both raise questions about equal protection under the Constitution and the extent to which the government can impose restrictions based on trans identity.

Roybal v. Griffith

Roybal v. Griffith involves Darlene Griffith, a trans woman who was incarcerated in an El Paso County, Colo., prison in 2020.

Griffith, who was assigned male at birth, was forced to be held in a men’s prison despite identifying as a trans woman. She was also denied access to woman’s undergarments and strip-searched by a male officer, despite requesting a female officer.

On Nov. 9, 2026, the Supreme Court vacated the lower court’s judgment, or canceled what the lower court had argued, sending the case to the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for further consideration following the recent decisions by the highest court in the land over West Virginia v. B.P.J. and United States v. Skrmetti. Both of those cases were considered a loss for the federal government stepping in to protect trans citizens.

These actions come directly after its June decision in West Virginia v. B.P.J., in which the justices addressed equal protection claims involving trans individuals and restrictions based on sex assigned at birth. The court sided with the exclusive policy holding that restricting female teams to biological females is substantially related to safety and competitive fairness.

In United States v. Skrmetti, the court held that policies restricting gender affirming care is on the basis of age — and not by sex (which has a higher standard to met) allowing the states to enact these laws, but not forcing them to do so.

Lawyers for the Trump-Vance administration, who submitted a brief supporting the Colorado prison, argued that the Supreme Court’s precedent on trans issues allows the government to separate biological males from female activities and spaces based on sex rather than gender identity.

“When a sex-based classification is justified as a constitutional matter’ – ‘for example,’ in ‘women’s and girls’ sports’ – then a state ‘may treat all biological males the same and treat all biological females the same’; it ‘is not constitutionally required to grant individualized exemptions to specific [persons] or subclasses,’” Solicitor General John Sauer wrote in a brief.

A lower federal court had previously found that Griffith’s equal protection rights were violated through her prison assignment and the prison’s failure to provide her with requested items. The court also disagreed with the prison’s strip-search policy.

Griffith’s attorneys pushed back against the administration’s arguments, saying the prison system already receives considerable deference from courts when making administrative decisions.

“The petition boils down to a plea for ‘administrative flexibility and deference,’ but prisons receive that regardless of the level of scrutiny applied to equal protection claims; deference in the unique context of prisons is baked into the analysis,” lawyers for Griffith wrote to the Supreme Court.

Talbott v. USA

Meanwhile, the Supreme Court is also being asked to take up Talbott v. USA, a case challenging the Trump-Vance administration’s categorical prohibition on trans military service.

President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14183, titled “Prioritizing Military Excellence and Readiness,” on Jan. 27, 2025, directing the Department of Defense to adopt policies prohibiting trans, nonbinary, and gender-nonconforming people from serving in the military.

The administration’s policy asserts that trans people are inherently incapable of meeting the military’s “high standards of readiness, lethality, cohesion, honesty, humility, uniformity, and integrity,” citing a history or signs of gender dysphoria. According to the Defense Department, this creates “medical, surgical, and mental health constraints on [an] individual.”

Under the policy, trans applicants are considered less qualified than their cisgender peers, regardless of their physical or intellectual capabilities.

On Tuesday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit denied the Trump-Vance administration’s request to halt a preliminary injunction blocking the military from discharging 27 trans service members who challenged the ban. The decision allows the injunction to take effect while the administration asks the Supreme Court to review the case.

Shannon Minter, legal director of the National Center for LGBTQ Rights, which represents the plaintiffs alongside GLAD Law and other law firms, said the ruling means the administration cannot enforce the ban against the 27 service members who brought the lawsuit.

“It immediately means that the Trump administration cannot enforce the ban against the plaintiffs in Talbott, against our 27 transgender service members who brought the case. They cannot be discharged from the military. They should be returned to active duty to their prior positions and, of course, permitted to adhere to the standards of their post-transition sex. They should be able to serve as themselves and be back at work.”

Minter said multiple federal courts have now found that the administration has failed to provide evidence justifying the ban, despite the government’s acknowledgment that the plaintiffs have served honorably and met military standards.

“We have had two federal district courts look at this issue and conclude that there is no evidence whatsoever to support a ban. The government concedes that the plaintiffs in these cases are serving honorably and meeting all standards. They’re doing, by any measure, an extraordinary job. There have been no issues with their service whatsoever.

“We’ve now had two federal appellate courts review those decisions and agree that the ban has no justification. The D.C. Circuit, for the second time, has looked at the evidence and concluded yet again that there’s no justification for the government to separate these individuals, who the government agrees have made our country safer.”

The Trump-Vance administration is still seeking Supreme Court intervention. Minter said the justices could consider the administration’s petition at their next conference in early December.

He argued that the administration’s legal strategy goes beyond trans military service and could establish a broader precedent giving the executive branch unchecked authority over military policy.

“The Trump administration is trying to get the Supreme Court to say that President Trump and the military can literally adopt any policies they wish, and that courts just have to defer to that. They’re betting that because this is a policy about a small, unpopular group, the Supreme Court is more likely to agree with that. But the impact of that would be much broader. It would be really devastating for our country if the Supreme Court held that Trump and Hegseth can literally impose any policy they wish on the military.”

Minter also disputed the administration’s characterization of the ban as a medical policy, arguing that it specifically targets trans people rather than evaluating service members individually based on their ability to perform their jobs.

“When you read the policy, it is very clear that the policy is targeted at transgender people because they are transgender. It has nothing to do with any medical condition.

“For every other medical condition, the military evaluates on an individual basis whether that has any bearing on someone’s ability to perform their job. One of the major goals of the military is to retain people once they’ve gone through the rigorous process of being screened and trained, as long as they can do the job.

“Gender dysphoria would be the only medical condition that results in immediate, automatic discharge, even for people who can continue to do the job. The policy is much broader than that, though. It says that everyone has to serve in their birth sex, which is just another way of saying you can’t be transgender.”

Nic Talbott, the trans service member whose name is attached to the military lawsuit, previously told the Washington Blade that being trans has never affected his ability to serve.

“Being transgender posed quite the obstacle to me achieving that dream,” Talbott told the Blade. “Not because it [being trans] had any bearing on my ability to become a soldier and meet the requirements of a United States soldier, but simply because of the policy changes that we’ve been facing as transgender service members throughout the course of the past decade … My being transgender had nothing to do with anything that I was doing as a soldier.”

Talbott also argued that having people with different backgrounds and experiences strengthens the military.

“I think the more diverse our military is, the stronger our military is … We need people from all different experiences and all different perspectives, because somebody is going to see that challenge or that problem in a way that I would never even think of … and that is what we need more of in the U.S. military.”

U.S. Supreme Court

Supreme Court weighs religious exemptions to LGBTQ nondiscrimination protections in Colo. preschool case

Ruling expected by June 2027

Published

3 weeks ago

on

November 3, 2026

By

Joe Reberkenny
An American and LGBTQ flag fly in front of the Supreme Court. (Washington Blade photo by Michael Key)

The U.S. Supreme Court heard oral arguments Tuesday in a case examining whether Colorado’s exclusion of religious preschools from a publicly funded education program violates the First Amendment’s guarantee of religious freedom.

In St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, Catholic preschools in Colorado have brought the fight to the nation’s highest court, arguing that their exclusion from the state’s universal preschool program, including its public funding, amounts to religious discrimination that violates their First Amendment rights.

The Catholic schools want to participate in the program and receive public funding while maintaining admissions policies that require families to support Catholic teachings on marriage, sexuality, and gender. Those policies conflict with the program’s equal-opportunity requirements, which prohibit discrimination based on characteristics including sexual orientation and gender identity.

Under the program, Colorado provides 15 hours of preschool per week for eligible children through participating public and private providers. The program allows families to select their preferred preschool, provided the school meets certain requirements, including equal-opportunity standards. The benefit has been valued at approximately $6,000 per child annually, according to attorneys representing the Catholic schools.

The plaintiffs in the case include St. Mary Catholic Parish, St. Bernadette Catholic Parish, the Archdiocese of Denver, and two parents of preschool-aged children. They went to federal court to challenge the state’s policy, arguing that making the Catholic preschools’ participation in the universal preschool program contingent on accepting the equal-opportunity requirements amounts to unlawful religious discrimination.

They argue that the First Amendment requires Colorado to provide a religious exemption to the nondiscrimination requirements so the schools can participate in the program without compromising their religious beliefs.

The schools also argue that Colorado permits certain enrollment preferences for secular purposes while refusing to accommodate their religious admissions policies.

The 10th U.S. Court of Appeals ruled in favor of Colorado in September 2025, upholding the state’s equal-opportunity requirements.

The 10th Circuit acknowledged that the Supreme Court has consistently held that states cannot categorically exclude religious institutions from otherwise available public benefits because of their religious character. However, it determined that Colorado was not explicitly excluding the schools because they were religious institutions. Rather, the schools were ineligible because their admissions policies did not comply with the program’s nondiscrimination requirements.

In the state’s view, these schools can participate in the preschool program provided they abide by the same equal-opportunity requirements imposed on other participating providers. Colorado argued that its restrictions apply to enrollment policies and conduct across the program and are not specifically targeted at religious institutions or religious practices.

The case requires the Supreme Court to consider several previous decisions involving religious freedom and the government’s ability to enforce generally applicable laws.

In 1990, the Supreme Court held in Employment Division v. Smith that neutral, generally applicable laws do not violate the First Amendment’s Free Exercise Clause simply because they place a burden on someone’s religious practices.

The case involved two men who worked at a private drug rehabilitation organization and were fired after ingesting peyote, a hallucinogenic substance, during a religious ceremony of the Native American Church. Oregon subsequently denied them unemployment benefits because their drug use constituted work-related misconduct. The Supreme Court ruled that the state’s denial did not violate their First Amendment rights.

Another ruling relevant to this case is the Supreme Court’s 2020 decision in Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue. The court ruled that Montana could not exclude religious schools from a generally available scholarship program solely because of their religious status. The decision held that doing so violated the Constitution’s Free Exercise Clause.

Another significant precedent is Carson v. Makin, in which the Supreme Court ruled in 2022 that Maine could not exclude religious schools from its public tuition-assistance program simply because they provided religious instruction. The state’s requirement that participating private schools be “nonsectarian” violated the First Amendment’s Free Exercise Clause.

The 6-3 decision was opposed by three justices, who argued that the ruling would require taxpayers to fund religious education and undermine the separation between church and state.

The Supreme Court’s decision in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy could further clarify how these precedents apply when states condition public funding on compliance with nondiscrimination requirements.

The court agreed to consider two specific questions: whether Colorado’s treatment of certain secular enrollment preferences undermines the general applicability of its nondiscrimination requirements under Employment Division v. Smith, and whether Carson v. Makin applies when the government does not explicitly exclude religious institutions from public benefits.

The ruling could have implications beyond Colorado’s preschool program, particularly for the ability of state and federal governments to enforce nondiscrimination requirements against religious organizations receiving public funding.

The Supreme Court is expected to issue a decision by the end of June 2027.

LGBTQ advocates weigh potential consequences

The Washington Blade spoke with Meg York, chief legal and policy officer of COLAGE, a national nonprofit organization that unites and supports people with LGBTQ parents. COLAGE filed an amicus brief in the case. York attended Tuesday’s oral arguments and discussed what she heard from the justices and the potential implications for LGBTQ families.

York emphasized that Colorado’s decision to include Catholic schools in its universal preschool program is an important distinction in the case, arguing that the dispute should not be characterized as a simple conflict between religious institutions and the state.

“Colorado explicitly chose to include Catholic schools in its universal pre-K program, so when we talk about the Catholic arguments, I think there’s maybe a false binary there that it’s one versus the other,” she told the Blade during a phone interview. “But in terms of the arguments raised by the petitioners or the respondents, I was listening to see if there was anybody who seemed to be kind of straying from what we typically expect in ideological lines, and I’m not sure that I heard that in this case.”

When asked how she interpreted the justices’ questions and what they could indicate about the eventual outcome, York said she saw some potential for the court to take a narrower approach that considers Colorado’s arguments.

“I do think that there were times at which I felt that some of the justices were potentially more receptive to really taking a more narrow approach to this case and really thinking about the arguments that Colorado was putting forward. I think there were some moments of hope. It’s hard when you’re in an oral argument. You hear some questions, but then there’s a lot of silence, too. It can be difficult to know which way certain folks are leaning or not.”

One of the central legal disputes involves whether Colorado’s equal-opportunity requirements are generally applicable or whether the state makes exceptions that could require it to accommodate religious admissions policies.

York disputed the characterization of the state’s provisions as exemptions, saying Colorado views them as measures intended to advance equal access rather than exceptions to its nondiscrimination requirements.

“I don’t think the state of Colorado was classifying them or framing them as exemptions as much as they were the kind of things that could advance their equal opportunity goals. So, you know, there were no exemptions to the nondiscrimination requirement, none at all. Colorado doesn’t give any exemptions to that. And so when they talk about schools that help serve low-income individuals or individuals with disabilities, those are all in furtherance of the equal opportunities that Colorado seeks to advance.”

The arguments also raised questions about how a ruling could affect nondiscrimination protections beyond the preschool program. Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson and Sonia Sotomayor raised concerns about how religious exemptions could affect laws designed to protect people based on characteristics such as sexual orientation and gender identity.

York pointed to those exchanges as particularly significant, questioning whether a broader interpretation of religious exemptions could subject more nondiscrimination laws to heightened constitutional scrutiny.

“Some of the concerns raised by Justice Jackson and also by Justice Sotomayor were about this idea of when you have protections or when you have a nondiscrimination law to protect people who have protected characteristics, that we’re not really in the business of determining whose belief is a sincerely held religious belief. So does that push everything to strict scrutiny? And I think there were some concerns about that.”

The case also puts two major lines of Supreme Court precedent under scrutiny: Employment Division v. Smith, the 1990 decision involving neutral, generally applicable laws, and Carson v. Makin, the 2022 decision prohibiting states from excluding religious schools from public benefits because of their religious instruction.

York noted that the justices grappled with how those decisions apply to Colorado’s program. She also emphasized that the Supreme Court declined to consider the plaintiffs’ separate request to overturn Employment Division v. Smith.

“In some ways, you have the petitioners who were kind of saying that the Carson line of cases is controlling, but then they were a little mushy in some of the cases being cited in that line of cases. We certainly heard the court grappling with what they consider when they’re considering Employment Division v. Smith. Does Carson make a reply here when you have very different circumstances under which that opinion was issued?”

For York, the case ultimately presents questions about how religious freedom and equal access can coexist, particularly when public funding is involved.

She said COLAGE believes LGBTQ families should be protected under nondiscrimination laws without requiring religious institutions to sacrifice their constitutional protections.

“My organization takes the position that religious freedom is something that we all value. Whether you are a specific religion or whether you are not religious, that is part of the freedoms that are guaranteed to us in the Constitution, and that’s something that benefits all of us. To that end, we feel that people with LGBTQ parents should be protected under the law, and that is exactly the heart of these nondiscrimination laws. And at the same time, that doesn’t mean that we need to sacrifice religious liberty or religious freedom to do so.”

York said she believes the case’s ultimate impact will depend heavily on how narrowly or broadly the justices write their decision.

“I don’t think it’s a foregone conclusion that they’re going to rule in favor of St. Mary or in favor of the petitioners, but even if they did, we could get a very narrow ruling that is incredibly specific and limited.”

LGBTQ organizations warn of consequences for families

Other LGBTQ advocacy organizations also warned that allowing religious preschools to participate in publicly funded programs while maintaining admissions policies that conflict with nondiscrimination requirements could have consequences for families beyond Colorado.

The National Women’s Law Center argued that a ruling in favor of the Catholic schools could undermine equal access to publicly funded education and potentially create a precedent for excluding other families.

“No four-year-old child should be denied preschool placement because their parents are gay or lesbian,” said Brian Dittmeier, director of LGBTQI+ equality at NWLC. “Marriage equality is the law of the land, and the court should not open the door to extreme arguments that seek to chip away at equal rights for same-sex couples. All families deserve access to affordable, high-quality early care and education, which is exactly why Colorado voters mobilized to expand early education access in their state through this universal and incredibly successful program.”

Dittmeier also said Colorado’s faith-based preschools have previously complied with nondiscrimination requirements and warned that allowing exceptions could leave same-sex families with fewer options.

“For years, Colorado’s faith-based preschools have had no trouble complying with nondiscrimination requirements as a common condition of receiving taxpayer funding to support their operations. Allowing discrimination in a state program specifically intended to achieve universal access is counter to Colorado voters’ intent and will leave same-sex families with fewer options to support their children. The same reasoning could later be used to turn away other children, including children of unmarried mothers or children whose parents are divorced. Such an outcome is unacceptable and will exacerbate the child care crisis in this country.”

The Human Rights Campaign similarly argued that public funding should not be used to discriminate against LGBTQ families.

“This case is straightforward — schools receiving public funds from a state universal preschool program cannot be allowed to use taxpayer dollars to leave LGBTQ+ families behind,” said HRC President Kelley Robinson. “As the arguments made clear today, Colorado’s non-discrimination requirement ensures no family can be denied a quality education simply for who they are — it is lawful and should be upheld. Exclusion has no place in our educational system.”

Lambda Legal and GLAD Law also filed a friend-of-the-court brief supporting Colorado.

During oral arguments, Colorado Deputy Solicitor General Helen Norton highlighted the practical consequences of allowing publicly funded schools to turn away families based on protected characteristics.

“Families are harmed when they’re turned away from the publicly-funded school that makes their lives work because of their protected class status,” Norton said. “Think of the parent who needs a school that opens at 7:00 A.M. so she can get the bus that takes her to work. Think of the parent who needs a school that will take all three of her kids so she doesn’t have to shuttle them among three different schools… For that parent to be turned away from those schools that make preschool possible for her family because of her protected status harms families and undermines Colorado’s interest.”

Karen Loewy, senior counsel and director of constitutional law practice at Lambda Legal, said religious schools can maintain their own admissions criteria when privately funded but should be required to follow state nondiscrimination laws when accepting taxpayer money.

“When the state pays schools to provide preschool programming, the schoolhouse door must be open to every family. While religious schools can set their own admissions criteria when they are privately funded, every school, religious or secular, that chooses to take taxpayer dollars is barred from discriminating in violation of Colorado law,” Loewy said. “No four-year-old should be turned away from a taxpayer-funded classroom because of who their parents are, including children of LGBTQ parents. Colorado’s requirements simply make sure public money isn’t used to discriminate, and the Constitution has long allowed states to set that condition.”

Archdiocese of Denver responds to concerns of LGBTQ discimination

The Blade also reached out to the Archdiocese of Denver for comment on its position in the case, particularly on how the ruling could affect LGBTQ families’ access to publicly funded educational programs.

The archdiocese responded by providing statements from some of the families involved in the case, who argued that they were fighting to end discrimination.

Dan and Lisa Sheley, Catholic parents of seven and Becket clients in the case, said, “Universal should mean everyone. Yet Colorado has barred families like ours from its universal preschool program simply because we chose a Catholic education for our children. We pray the Supreme Court will end this discrimination and hold Colorado to its word.”

Nicholas Reaves, senior counsel at Becket and lead attorney for the families and preschools, emphasized past decisions from the Supreme Court that sided with religious groups in disputes over public benefits. He argued that religious schools should not have to abandon their beliefs to receive those benefits.

“Colorado’s Catholics-need-not-apply rules make a mockery of our nation’s laws and commitment to religious freedom,” Reaves said. “The Supreme Court has been crystal clear: Americans don’t have to forfeit their faith to receive public benefits. We are confident that this discrimination won’t stand and that the court will hand Colorado yet another loss.”

U.S. Supreme Court

Supreme Court blocks White House anti-trans prison policy

Justices side with trans inmates who challenged Trump-Vance administration directive

Published

1 month ago

on

October 21, 2026

By

Joe Reberkenny
LGBTQ Rights protesters outside of the Supreme Court. (Washington Blade photo by Michael Key)

The U.S. Supreme Court has blocked a Trump-Vance administration policy that would have ended gender-affirming care for prisoners.

On Wednesday, the justices rejected an emergency application filed by the administration that would have allowed the Bureau of Prisons to restrict gender-affirming care for transgender inmates in federal prisons.

Three prisoners, Alishea Kingdom, Jas Kapule and Solo Nichols, have said they had been receiving hormone therapy for years as inmates and challenged the sudden policy change. They argued that the abrupt change to decades of policy would end treatment for nearly 1,000 people in custody. The assertion of security concerns within prisons, the American Civil Liberties Union told the Supreme Court, was odd “given that BOP has not pointed to a single security incident relating to its provision of this treatment over the past 30 years.”

According to the application, President Donald Trump’s order called on the Bureau of Prisons to revise its medical care policies so that federal funds aren’t spent “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.”

Two justices, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, would have allowed the policy to be enforced but ultimately did not join the majority, marking a rare judicial win for trans people at the nation’s highest court.

This decision is in line with other anti-trans actions taken by the White House regarding inmate rights. In May, the Washington Blade first reported on letters from congressional Democrats condemning changes to official BOP policy regarding trans inmates to bring it in line with Trump’s Executive Order 14168, titled “Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government.”

The policy would require BOP staff to “refer to individuals by their legal name or pronouns corresponding to their biological sex,” ban the use of funds for any “items that align with transgender ideology,” and suspend clothing accommodations, pat-search accommodations, and support programs offered to trans individuals.

The BOP responded to the Blade’s request for additional information about its policy change, but BOP spokesperson Donald Murphy said the updated policy is “rooted in medical guidance” and “data-driven decision making,” despite the guidance running counter to what most doctors who specialize in trans health care would recommend.

In June, the court upheld state bans on trans athletes participating in women’s and girls’ sports. A year earlier, the court upheld state laws banning gender-transition treatments for trans youth.

The court has also allowed Trump to implement a ban on trans people serving in the military.

Human Rights Campaign President Kelley Robinson sent a statement to the Blade following the court’s decision.

“Today, trans people in federal prisons can keep getting the care they need. Denying access to critical medical care for incarcerated people simply because they are trans is discriminatory, cruel and flies in the face of our Eighth Amendment protections,” Robinson said via email. “Trump and MAGA extremists are obsessed with targeting our community and undermining access to essential healthcare, defying the recommendations of every major medical association in the country. This decision protects incarcerated trans people from the administration’s attempt to steamroll over constitutional rights for now, but the fight to uphold the dignity and respect our community deserves is far from over.”

The White House responded to the Blade’s request for comment on the decision, calling the order a “loss for common sense.”

“Since the President’s very first day in office, he has fought to halt the U.S. taxpayer funding of transgender mutilation of prison inmates, and the waste of taxpayer resources on so-called ‘social accommodations,'” White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster told the Blade. “This administration will continue to fight for bold action to stop the waste of taxpayer dollars, restore Gold Standard Science as the guiding principle of all health policy, and protect countless Americans from these dangerous, life-altering medical practices, especially those funded on the taxpayer’s tab.”
